reference_drawer.title: 📖 Consistency Reference Guide
reference_drawer.description: Essential rules for classifying a pair of linear equations:

items.rule: Write each equation as a₁x+b₁y+c₁=0 before comparing corresponding coefficients.
Unequal x- and y-coefficient ratios indicate one common solution.
Equal x- and y-coefficient ratios with a different constant ratio indicate parallel distinct lines.
Equal ratios for all three corresponding coefficients indicate coincident lines.
One solution means intersecting lines; no solution means parallel lines; infinitely many means coincident lines.
items.example: Two coincident lines share every point.

concepts.title: 1. What does consistency mean?
concepts.subtitle: Existence of a common solution
concepts.summary: A pair is consistent if it has at least one solution.

points.text: Consistent: One or infinitely many common solutions.

concepts.trap: Consistent does not mean only one solution.

concepts.title: 2. The three solution cases
concepts.subtitle: Unique, none, or infinitely many
concepts.summary: Two linear equations can represent intersecting, parallel, or coincident lines.
concepts.trap: Never call a no-solution pair 'inconsistent with one solution'.

concepts.title: 3. Coefficient-ratio conditions
concepts.subtitle: The algebraic classification test
concepts.summary: Compare the three corresponding coefficient ratios after standardising both equations.

points.text: Infinitely many: all three ratios are equal.

concepts.trap: Equal first two ratios alone do not distinguish parallel from coincident lines.

concepts.title: 4. Standardise before comparing
concepts.subtitle: Signs and placement matter
concepts.summary: Equivalent equations should be written in one compatible form before ratios are compared.

points.text: Move terms consistently: Put all terms on one side.
Preserve signs: A sign error changes the ratio test.

concepts.trap: Do not compare coefficients from mismatched forms without standardising.

worked_examples.title: Type 1: Unique Solution
worked_examples.problem: Determine the nature of the solutions of 2x+3y−5=0 and 4x−y+7=0.

steps.statement: Compare x and y coefficient ratios.
steps.reason: These are the first two ratios in the consistency test.
Unequal x- and y-coefficient ratios mean the lines have different slopes.
Lines with different slopes intersect at one point.

worked_examples.conclusion: The pair is consistent with a unique solution.

worked_examples.title: Type 2: No Solution
worked_examples.problem: Determine the nature of the solutions of 2x+4y−7=0 and x+2y+3=0.

steps.statement: Compare x and y coefficient ratios.
steps.reason: The first two ratios are equal, so the lines have the same slope.
The constant ratio is different from the common coefficient ratio.
Equal x/y ratios with a different constant ratio give parallel distinct lines.

worked_examples.conclusion: The pair is inconsistent and has no solution.

worked_examples.title: Type 3: Infinitely Many Solutions
worked_examples.problem: Determine the nature of the solutions of 2x+4y−6=0 and x+2y−3=0.

steps.reason: The y-coefficient ratio matches the x-coefficient ratio.
All three corresponding ratios are equal.
The equations represent the same line.

worked_examples.conclusion: The pair is consistent with infinitely many solutions.

worked_examples.title: Type 4: Standardise Before Testing
worked_examples.problem: Determine the nature of the solutions of x+y=5 and 2x+2y=10.

steps.statement: Write both equations in standard form.
steps.reason: The ratio test compares a₁,b₁,c₁ with a₂,b₂,c₂.

worked_examples.conclusion: The pair is consistent with infinitely many solutions.

mastery_contract.definition: Mastery means reliably classifying a pair of linear equations using standard form, coefficient ratios, and the geometric meaning of the solution cases.
mastery_contract.duplicate_policy: Repeated attempts on the same question do not create additional distinct-question mastery evidence.

student_experience.principle: Keep the learner focused on the pattern: standardise → compare ratios → classify.
student_experience.first_wrong_message: Not quite. Check the ratio pattern and try again.
student_experience.second_wrong_message: Let's review the consistency condition behind that step.
student_experience.remediation_message: Let's strengthen this classification skill, then return to your question.
student_experience.mastered_message: 🎉 You've mastered consistency of a pair of linear equations.

interaction_contract.mobile_rule: One strategy choice → one guided calculation → feedback → next move.

principles: Avoid completed-question repeats while fresh items remain.
Fade guidance from strategy to guided calculation to notebook solve.
Do not increase difficulty and reduce support simultaneously without strong evidence.
Prefer questions that supply missing skill or typology evidence.

skill_taxonomy.coefficient_ratio_test: Calculate and compare corresponding coefficient ratios.
skill_taxonomy.solution_case_classification: Distinguish unique, no, and infinitely many solutions.
skill_taxonomy.geometric_solution_interpretation: Connect algebraic cases to intersecting, parallel, and coincident lines.

atomic_step_contract.unlock_rule: A step unlocks only after the immediately preceding step is correctly completed.
atomic_step_contract.retry_rule: Wrong response retries the current step only; prior completed steps remain preserved.
atomic_step_contract.partial_field_rule: For multi-field steps, every required field must be correct before the step unlocks.
atomic_step_contract.hint_rule: Hints and remediation apply to the current step only and cannot unlock a future step.
atomic_step_contract.adaptive_rule: Adaptive question selection may choose another question, but it may not bypass an incomplete mathematical prerequisite step.
atomic_step_contract.evidence_rule: Record skill evidence against the atomic step actually completed; never award downstream skill evidence for skipped upstream work.
